title: 1.1.22 Describe the Lifecycle
description: Describe the four framework activities, walk a real product through them, and map them onto the five-phase naming. AI-graded with hints.

aiGrader.prompt:
Everything you need is in the 1.1.5 video, 1.1.6 (The Four Phases), the worked example in 1.1.8, and 1.1.10 (Umbrella Activities): go back and reread or rewatch if you get stuck. Your own everyday words throughout.

Part 1: Describe the four framework activities: inception, elaboration, construction and deployment. One or two sentences each about what happens in that activity. (1.1.5 and 1.1.6)

Part 2: Pick one real software product you actually use: Instagram, Spotify, Google Maps, Roblox, YouTube, Google Docs, anything. Name it, then walk it through all four activities, saying what you think happened in each one for that product. Best-guess reasoning is fine; no research needed. (1.1.8 shows this done for a greeting app)

Part 3: Name at least one umbrella activity, and say in one sentence why it runs across all four phases instead of sitting inside one of them. (1.1.10)

Part 4: Two namings, one lifecycle. The 1.1.5 video counts five phases (design, development, testing, deployment, maintenance); 1.1.6 counts four framework activities. They describe the same lifecycle. Name the two phases the four-activity list does not give a name of its own to, and say in one sentence each where that work happens in the four-activity view. (1.1.6, the table on this page)

rubric.title: All four phases named and described
rubric.description: Student names and describes all four framework activities: inception, elaboration, construction, deployment. Credit is generous per phase - a brief, even one-phrase description is enough, it doesn't need to be precise or complete. Full credit for all four named with some description, however short. If one of the four is missing entirely or named with no description at all, treat it as partial rather than denying the whole criterion.

rubric.title: One named real product
rubric.description: Student names one real software product they use (e.g. a specific app, game, or service). Any recognizable name counts, spelled however the student spells it. Credit generously; withhold credit only if no actual name appears anywhere (just 'an app' or 'a website' with nothing more specific).

rubric.title: One concrete sentence per phase for that product
rubric.description: Student gives at least one concrete sentence per phase for the named product, saying what probably happened in that phase for it. Credit a sentence as concrete even if it's a rough guess or thin - the point is that it's actually about the named product, not phase-content accuracy. Full credit for all four phases covered. If one phase is thin or missing while the other three are solid, treat it as partial rather than denying the whole criterion.

rubric.title: At least one umbrella activity mentioned by name
rubric.description: Student mentions at least one umbrella activity, even paraphrased rather than the exact course term (e.g. quality management, security management, risk management, configuration management, architecture management, training/communication). A close variant like 'security' or 'making sure it works well throughout' counts if it clearly points at one of these. Credit generously; withhold only if nothing resembling an umbrella activity appears anywhere.

rubric.title: Own words
rubric.description: The response is written in the student's own words, not copied from a source. Withhold credit only for significant issues: text that reads as copied/dictionary-style, or writing too disorganized to follow. Do not withhold for length: a short response that clearly covers the four phases and a product walkthrough is fine. This is not a prose-quality score.

rubric.title: Maps the four activities onto the five-phase naming
rubric.description: Student identifies testing and maintenance as the two phases the four-activity list does not name separately, and says roughly where each one lives - testing running across the phases (or inside construction), maintenance continuing after deployment. Credit naming both with any reasonable placement, even a vague one. Naming both but placing only one still earns it. Credit only one of the two named as partial rather than missing.
